chapters.title: Chapter 3: Switching Costs and Network Effects

lessons.title: Switching Costs: Why Customers Stay Even When Rivals Are Cheaper

body.text: The best customer is not the one who loves you. It is the one for whom leaving would be too expensive, too risky, or too painful to bother.

children.text: A rival offers the same service at 15% less. In most industries, customers would move. In businesses protected by switching costs, they stay, and not because they are loyal. They stay because the cost, effort, and risk of changing outweigh the saving. That inertia lets a company hold prices, keep customers for decades, and earn high returns without having the best price in the market.
What Counts as a Switching Cost

markDefs.definition: Any cost a customer bears when moving from one supplier to another: money, time, retraining, disruption, or risk. High switching costs lock customers in even when a cheaper alternative exists.

children.text: A
switching cost
is anything the customer loses or must spend by changing supplier. Not all of it shows up as a fee.

body.caption: The four types of switching costs, with Indian examples

cells: Direct costs of leaving: fees, penalties, taxes, or lost accumulated benefits
Redeeming a mutual fund to move to another AMC can trigger exit loads and capital gains tax
Time and effort to migrate data, retrain staff, and rebuild processes
Banks running core banking software from Oracle Financial Services Software or Intellect Design Arena rarely replace it, because migration touches every account and branch
The danger that something breaks during the change, hurting the customer's own business
A global bank outsourcing critical systems to TCS or Infosys risks outages and errors if it changes vendor mid-stream
Formal approvals or testing needed before a new supplier can be used

A pharma company that changes its API supplier may need regulatory approval, which keeps established suppliers like Divi's Laboratories in place; auto parts suppliers are typically locked in for the life of a vehicle platform

children.text: The Customer's Math
Switching costs work because customers run a quiet cost-benefit calculation, even if they never write it down. Here is one written out.
Example: A Mid-Size Bank Considers New Core Banking Software

stats.label: One-time migration cost
stats.context: Data migration, testing, parallel running, training

stats.label: Unpriced risk
stats.context: Outages, errors, RBI scrutiny, customer complaints

children.text: A six-year payback, plus the risk of a failed migration that could damage customer trust and attract regulatory attention, is an easy decision for the bank's board: stay. The existing vendor knows this. It can raise prices modestly each year, and the bank will still stay, as long as the increase never makes switching look clearly worth it.

body.text: Switching cost moats are strongest when the product is a small part of the customer's total costs but critical to their operations. Core banking software is a small line in a bank's budget, and a failure would be catastrophic. That combination makes price increases easy to accept and switching very hard to justify.

children.text: Why Retention Is Worth So Much

markDefs.definition: The percentage of customers lost in a period. Annual churn of 5% means 5 out of every 100 customers leave each year.

children.text: For the company, switching costs show up as low
churn
. Small differences in churn compound into huge differences in how long a customer stays and how much profit they generate.

body.caption: Assumes a constant churn rate each year

body.title: Share of Original Customers Still Remaining (%)

children.text: After ten years, a business with 95% annual retention still has about 60% of its original customers. One with 80% retention has about 11%, and must spend heavily just to replace the customers it loses. That replacement spending is exactly what switching costs save.
Customers remaining after t years = retention rate^t.
95% retention: 0.95^10 = 0.599, or about 60% remaining.
90% retention: 0.90^10 = 0.349, or about 35% remaining.
80% retention: 0.80^10 = 0.107, or about 11% remaining.

Average lifetime: 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 years at 5% churn; 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5 years at 20% churn. If each customer generates ₹1 lakh of profit a year, the undiscounted lifetime profit is ₹20 lakh versus ₹5 lakh, four times as much from the same customer.

body.title: Calculate Customer Lifetime
body.prompt: A B2B software company loses 8% of its customers every year. Assuming churn stays constant, what is the average customer lifetime in years?
body.explanation: Average lifetime = 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5 years. If a competitor with stronger switching costs had 4% churn, its average customer would stay 25 years, double the lifetime from the same kind of customer.

children.text: High vs Low Switching Cost Businesses

body.title: Where switching costs protect profits, and where they do not

columns.label: High switching costs
points: IT services running mission-critical client systems
Approved API suppliers to regulated pharma customers
Auto components designed into a vehicle platform
Specialty chemicals built into a customer's formulation

columns.label: Low switching costs
points: Stock brokers, since demat holdings can be transferred between brokers
Consumer apps with free, similar alternatives

body.text: Regulators often lower switching costs deliberately to help consumers. Nationwide mobile number portability, launched in India in 2011, removed the pain of changing your phone number when switching telecom operators. UPI made moving money between banks instant. When evaluating a switching cost moat, always ask whether a regulator has a reason to make switching easier.

children.text: Where Switching Cost Moats Get Tested
Contract renewals:
large IT services and software deals are periodically re-bid. Switching costs help the incumbent, but aggressive pricing from rivals at renewal can still force discounts.
Technology platform shifts:
when customers must migrate anyway, for example from on-premise systems to cloud platforms, the incumbent loses its lock-in because the switching cost is being paid regardless.
Overpricing:
a company that exploits lock-in too aggressively gives customers a reason to finally absorb the switching cost.
Vendor consolidation:
large clients sometimes cut their vendor list, which can remove a smaller supplier regardless of how embedded it was.
How to Spot Switching Costs in Disclosures
Long client relationships: IT services companies often disclose the number of clients in revenue bands such as $100 million and above, and how many years top clients have stayed.
Repeat business: a high share of revenue coming from existing customers year after year.
Stable or rising pricing on renewals, mentioned in concall transcripts.
High and steady ROCE with relatively low sales and marketing spend, because the company does not need to keep buying new customers.

body.title: Where Are Switching Costs Highest?
body.question: Which customer faces the highest switching cost?
options: A retail investor moving their trading account from one discount broker to another
A salaried professional changing their mobile operator today
A US generic drug maker whose approved product filing names a specific Indian API supplier
A family choosing a different biscuit brand next month
body.explanation: Changing a named API supplier in a regulated drug filing can require regulatory approval, testing, and time, with the risk of supply disruption. Moving brokers and changing mobile operators have been made easy by demat transfers and number portability. Changing biscuit brands costs nothing.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: Switching cost moats are strongest when the product is a small part of the customer's costs but ___ to the customer's operations.
body.explanation: When a product is cheap relative to the customer's budget but its failure would be very damaging, the customer has little incentive to switch for a small saving.

body.title: The Cloud Migration Threat
body.scenario: You own shares in a listed Indian software company that sells on-premise lending software to about 150 banks and NBFCs across Asia and Africa. Churn has been under 3% a year for a decade, and ROCE is consistently above 30%. Over the next five years, many of its clients plan to move their systems to the cloud. Global cloud-native lending platforms are pitching these clients aggressively.
body.prompt: How does the planned cloud migration affect this company's switching cost moat? What would you monitor?
body.modelAnswer: The cloud migration is a genuine threat, because the company's moat rests on migration being expensive and risky. If clients must migrate anyway, the switching cost is paid regardless of vendor, so the decision reopens and cloud-native rivals get a fair shot. The moat is not destroyed, since the incumbent still has deep knowledge of client processes and data, and can offer its own cloud version with a smoother migration. What to monitor: whether the company has a credible cloud product and how many existing clients adopt it; churn during the migration years compared with the historical 3%; pricing on renewals and any discounts offered to retain clients; new client wins against cloud-native competitors; and ROCE and margins as the business model shifts. If existing clients migrate to the company's own cloud offering at similar pricing, the moat survives the transition. If churn rises and renewals come with steep discounts, the moat is narrowing.

body.text: Companies named are used to illustrate concepts from public information and are not investment recommendations. The core banking and cloud software examples are hypothetical.

points: Switching costs keep customers in place even when a rival is cheaper, because leaving costs more than the saving
They come in four forms: financial, procedural and learning, operational risk, and regulatory or qualification
The moat is strongest when the product is a small share of the customer's costs but critical to their operations
Low churn compounds: 95% annual retention keeps about 60% of customers after 10 years, while 80% keeps about 11%
Regulators often reduce switching costs deliberately, as mobile number portability and UPI did
Switching cost moats get tested at contract renewals, technology platform shifts, and when companies overprice their lock-in
